questions.stem: What does the Snowflake Native App Framework allow providers to do?

options.text: Only replicate data across regions
Create data applications that share data and related business logic with other Snowflake accounts
Provision reader accounts automatically
Manage virtual warehouse scaling policies

explanation.correct: The Native App Framework lets providers create data applications that share data and related business logic (Streamlit apps, stored procedures, functions) with other Snowflake accounts.

distractors.A: Cross-region replication is a separate feature, not the purpose of the Native App Framework.
distractors.C: The framework is not about provisioning reader accounts.
distractors.D: It is not a warehouse scaling tool.

questions.stem: What is an application package in the Native App Framework?

options.text: A consumer's installed application object
A resource monitor for the app's compute
A container that encapsulates the data content, application logic, metadata, and setup script for an app
A listing profile

explanation.correct: An application package encapsulates the data content, application logic, metadata, and setup script required by an application, plus version and patch information.

distractors.A: The consumer's installed object is the Snowflake Native App (application object), not the package.
distractors.B: It is not a resource monitor.
distractors.D: It is not a listing profile.

questions.stem: Which TWO files/components does an application package require? (Select TWO)

options.text: A resource monitor definition
A manifest file
A setup script
A reader account configuration
A replication group

explanation.correct: An application package requires a manifest file (defines configuration/setup properties, including the setup script location and versions) and a setup script (SQL run on install/upgrade).

distractors.A: A resource monitor is not a required app package component.
distractors.D: A reader account configuration is unrelated to app packages.
distractors.E: A replication group is a DR construct, not part of an app package.

questions.stem: What does the setup script in an application package contain?

options.text: The consumer's billing details
The provider's cloud credentials
SQL statements run when the consumer installs or upgrades the application (or the provider installs it for testing)
A list of allowed IP addresses

explanation.correct: The setup script contains SQL statements that run when a consumer installs or upgrades an application, or when a provider installs/upgrades it for testing. Its location is specified in the manifest file.

distractors.A: The setup script does not contain consumer billing details.
distractors.B: It does not contain provider cloud credentials.
distractors.D: It is not an IP allowlist.

questions.scenario: A consumer inspects what object gets created in their account when they install a Native App.
questions.stem: What is a Snowflake Native App (the application object)?

options.text: The listing metadata shown on the Marketplace
The database object installed in the consumer account when they install the app
The provider's source-control repository
A secure view in the provider account

explanation.correct: A Snowflake Native App is the database object installed in the consumer account; when installed, Snowflake creates the application and runs the setup script to create the required objects within it.

distractors.A: Listing metadata is separate from the installed application object.
distractors.C: The provider's source control holds code files, not the installed app object.
distractors.D: It is a full application object, not merely a secure view.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about publishing a Native App are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Native Apps can only be shared using direct shares
Publishing an app requires copying the app into each consumer account manually
The app is shared with consumers by publishing a listing with the application package as the data product
The listing can be a Snowflake Marketplace listing or a private listing
Native App listings cannot be monetized

explanation.correct: A provider shares an app by publishing a listing that has the application package as its data product; the listing can be a Marketplace listing or a private listing.

distractors.A: Apps are distributed via listings, not direct shares.
distractors.B: No manual copying into consumer accounts is required.
distractors.E: Native App listings can be free or paid (monetizable).

questions.scenario: A provider wants to change and evolve their application's logic and release updates incrementally to consumers.
questions.stem: Which Native App Framework capability supports this?

options.text: Reader account cloning
Cross-region failover
Time Travel on the consumer database
The ability to release versions and patches for the application

explanation.correct: The framework lets providers release versions and patches, allowing them to change and evolve the app's logic and release incrementally to consumers.

distractors.A: Reader account cloning is not how app logic is evolved.
distractors.B: Failover is a DR feature, unrelated to app version releases.
distractors.C: Time Travel does not manage app versioning.

questions.scenario: A provider prepares to publish an application package to accounts outside their organization.
questions.stem: What triggers the automated security scan required for external distribution?

options.text: Granting IMPORTED PRIVILEGES to the consumer
Setting the DISTRIBUTION property of the application package to EXTERNAL
Creating a reader account
Enabling Tri-Secret Secure

explanation.correct: The automated security scan is initiated when you set the DISTRIBUTION property of the application package to EXTERNAL (or add a new version/patch to a package already set to EXTERNAL).

distractors.A: IMPORTED PRIVILEGES concerns consumer access to shared databases, not the security scan.
distractors.C: Creating a reader account does not trigger the scan.
distractors.D: Tri-Secret Secure is an encryption feature, unrelated to triggering the scan.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about the Native App listing approval flow are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Native App listings never undergo any review
If the automated security scan fails, Snowflake performs a manual security review (approximately 3 business days)
An app using Snowpark Container Services requires completing a security questionnaire before the scan
A failed review cannot be corrected or resubmitted
The security scan is skipped for external distribution

explanation.correct: If the automated security scan fails, Snowflake performs a manual security review (~3 business days). If the app uses SPCS, you must complete a security questionnaire before the automated scan starts.

distractors.A: Native App listings undergo metadata review and a functional review.
distractors.D: A rejected listing can be updated based on feedback and resubmitted.
distractors.E: The security scan is required for external distribution, not skipped.

questions.scenario: A provider's Native App listing on the Marketplace is rejected during review.
questions.stem: Approximately how long can Native App reviews take, and how is feedback delivered?

options.text: Reviews always complete in under 1 hour with in-app feedback
Reviews take exactly 90 days with no feedback
Reviews may take up to 14 days; feedback goes to the business and technical contact emails in the profile
Rejections are never communicated

explanation.correct: For Native App listings, reviews may take up to 14 days; if rejected, Snowflake reaches out using the business and technical contact emails in the profile with feedback.

distractors.A: Reviews are not sub-hour; Native App reviews can take up to 14 days.
distractors.B: Reviews are up to 14 days, not a fixed 90 days, and feedback is provided.
distractors.D: Rejections are communicated via the profile contact emails.

questions.scenario: A provider must set which version or patch of the app a published listing points to.
questions.stem: What must be specified before creating a listing for an application package?

options.text: A resource monitor threshold
A Tri-Secret Secure key
A failover group
The default release directive (pointing to the version/patch being published)

explanation.correct: Before creating a listing for an application package, you must specify the default release directive that points to the version or patch of the app you are publishing.

distractors.A: A resource monitor is unrelated to publishing an app version.
distractors.B: A Tri-Secret Secure key is not required to set the published version.
distractors.C: A failover group is a DR construct, not a release directive.

questions.scenario: A provider sets up roles and privileges to create and manage a listing for an application package.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about the required roles/privileges are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: You can transfer the OWNERSHIP privilege for a share
The listing owner needs only the SELECT privilege
The role that attaches a data product to a listing and publishes it must be the same role that owns the application package
If a different role manages the listing, grant it the MODIFY privilege on the listing
No privileges are required to publish a listing

explanation.correct: The role that attaches the data product and publishes the listing must be the role that owns the application package/share. If a different role manages the listing, grant it the MODIFY privilege on the listing (you cannot transfer OWNERSHIP for a share).

distractors.A: You cannot transfer the OWNERSHIP privilege for a share.
distractors.B: The listing owner needs OWNERSHIP on the listing and the global CREATE LISTING privilege, not just SELECT.
distractors.E: Publishing a listing requires specific privileges.

questions.scenario: A provider wants to test their application before publishing it broadly, to speed up the review process.
questions.stem: A provider wants to speed up the review process before publishing. Which TWO recommendations/statements are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Skip testing to save time
Test the app by privately sharing it with another account before submitting for publishing
Publish publicly first, then test afterward
Private testing may expedite the review process
Test only in a consumer's production account

explanation.correct: Snowflake recommends testing the app by privately sharing it with another account before submitting for publishing, which may expedite the review process.

distractors.C: Testing should occur before public publishing.
distractors.E: Testing does not require a consumer's production account; single-account testing is supported.

questions.scenario: A consumer works with a Snowflake Native App after installing it.
questions.stem: Which THREE actions can a consumer perform with an installed Native App? (Select THREE)

options.text: Directly edit the provider's application source code
Transfer ownership of the app package to another provider
Use the app by accessing data via Snowflake worksheets
View Streamlit apps created by the provider
Share event and logging information with the provider
Bypass the app's declared privilege requirements

explanation.correct: Consumers can use the app via Snowflake worksheets, view provider Streamlit apps, grant privileges/associate references, and share event and logging information with the provider.

distractors.A: Consumers cannot edit the provider's application source code.
distractors.B: Consumers cannot transfer ownership of the provider's application package.
distractors.F: Consumers grant the app's required privileges; they do not bypass them.

questions.scenario: A consumer follows the typical workflow for working with a Snowflake Native App.
questions.stem: Which TWO steps are part of the consumer workflow? (Select TWO)

options.text: Install the app from a listing
Review the app's access requests (grant privileges and create references)
Publish the app to the Marketplace
Run the automated security scan
Set the app's default release directive

explanation.correct: The consumer workflow includes becoming a consumer, installing the app from a listing, reviewing access requests (granting privileges and creating references), and optionally setting up an event table for logging.

distractors.C: Publishing to the Marketplace is a provider action, not a consumer step.
distractors.D: Running the security scan is a provider action.
distractors.E: Setting the release directive is a provider action.

questions.scenario: A consumer wants to help the provider troubleshoot the installed app by sharing logs.
questions.stem: What optional step enables logging and event sharing for the app?

options.text: Create a resource monitor
Set up an event table
Grant OWNERSHIP of the app to the provider
Enable Tri-Secret Secure

explanation.correct: As an optional step, the consumer sets up an event table to enable logging and event sharing for the app, helping the provider troubleshoot.

distractors.A: A resource monitor governs credit usage, not logging/event sharing.
distractors.C: Consumers do not grant OWNERSHIP of the app to the provider.
distractors.D: Tri-Secret Secure is encryption, not app logging.

questions.scenario: A consumer installed an app from a limited trial listing and the trial period is ending.
questions.stem: What happens if the consumer does not convert the app to a full listing?

options.text: The app continues indefinitely for free
The app is immediately deleted with all its data
Snowflake automatically suspends the app (after sending an expiry notification)
The provider is billed for continued access

explanation.correct: When the trial period ends, Snowflake automatically suspends the app unless the consumer converts it to a full listing; a notification is sent before suspension. Snowflake recommends converting before expiry.

distractors.A: The app does not continue free indefinitely; it is suspended.
distractors.B: Data written inside the app is retained as long as the consumer doesn't delete the app; it is not immediately deleted.
distractors.D: The provider is not billed to continue the consumer's trial access.

questions.scenario: A trial app that created objects in the consumer account (outside the application object) is about to be uninstalled, and the consumer wants to keep those objects.
questions.stem: What must the consumer do?

options.text: Nothing; all objects are always retained automatically
Re-run the security scan
Ask the provider to publish a new version
Transfer ownership of those objects before uninstalling the app

explanation.correct: If a trial app created objects in the consumer account outside the application object, consumers can retain them after uninstalling only if they transfer ownership of those objects before uninstalling the app.

distractors.A: Objects outside the app object require ownership transfer to be retained through uninstall.
distractors.B: Re-running the security scan is a provider action and does not retain objects.
distractors.C: A new provider version does not retain the consumer's external objects on uninstall.

questions.scenario: A team evaluates the enhanced development experience of the Native App Framework.
questions.stem: Which TWO development experience benefits does the framework provide? (Select TWO)

options.text: Automatic elimination of all compute costs
A streamlined testing environment where you can test applications from a single account
The ability to manage supporting code files and resources in source control
Direct write access to consumer production data
Guaranteed instant Marketplace approval

explanation.correct: The framework provides a streamlined single-account testing environment and a robust developer workflow where data/objects stay in Snowflake while supporting code files and resources are managed in source control.

distractors.A: The framework does not eliminate all compute costs.
distractors.D: It does not grant direct write access to consumer production data.
distractors.E: Approval is not instant or guaranteed; listings undergo review.

questions.scenario: A provider builds a Native App that runs containerized workloads in Snowflake.
questions.stem: What is this type of app called, and what does it leverage?

options.text: A reader account app with no framework features
A direct-share container with external hosting
A Snowflake Native App with Snowpark Container Services, leveraging the framework's features (IP protection, security, data sharing, monetization)
A replication container for failover

explanation.correct: A Snowflake Native App with Snowpark Container Services runs container workloads in Snowflake and leverages all the framework's features, including provider IP protection, security/governance, data sharing, monetization, and compute integration.

distractors.A: It is a full framework app, not a feature-less reader account app.
distractors.B: It runs in Snowflake via SPCS, not external hosting through a direct share.
distractors.D: It is not a replication/failover container.
